name: Koenji
tagline: Eight minutes to Shinjuku and cheap with it — because the housing is dense timber-built stock and because the Chuo Line is packed in the morning.
summary: The JR Chuo Line Rapid reaches Shinjuku in eight minutes and Tokyo in twenty-two. Vintage clothing shops, live music venues and owner-run restaurants cluster here, and the neighbourhood has more character of its own than almost any residential area in Tokyo. Rent is clearly lower than elsewhere along the Chuo Line, and the reasons are the high proportion of timber-built flats and the Chuo Line's crowding and frequent delays in the morning. On weekends and holidays the Rapid does not stop here at all, leaving only the local trains — something a fair number of people discover only after moving in.

faces.morning: The Chuo Line in the morning is one of the most crowded stretches in Tokyo, and by Koenji the inbound trains already have no room. Delays happen chronically, so if your workplace is strict about start times, allow extra every morning. Outside the station from seven onwards, people come through the gates and keep moving without stopping.
faces.daytime: The vintage shops and cafes open around midday, so the shopping streets are quieter in the morning than you might expect. On weekday afternoons the residential streets and the shopping streets blend, and the roads feel lived-in.
faces.night: Many bars stay open until late, and there are still people about after the last train. For a residential part of Tokyo, restaurants close unusually late here, which does not suit anyone looking for quiet.
faces.weekend: Visitors come for the vintage clothing and the shopping streets get busy. During the Awa Odori dance festival at the end of August, the whole neighbourhood fills with dancers and spectators for several days, and residents find it hard to get out to the shops. The Rapid passes through and only local trains stop, so getting anywhere takes longer than on a weekday.

terrain.note: The station sits on the Musashino terrace at 42 m above sea level, with only about 7 m of variation within 800 m. Getting around by bicycle is easy, and cycling is a realistic way to reach Nakano and Asagaya. The ground does slope gently down to the south, towards the Kanda River.

noiseSources: Along the Chuo Line viaduct, trains can be heard until the last service
Kanpachi-dori to the south and Ome-kaido to the north carry traffic continuously

exits.name: North exit (北口)
exits.line: JR Chuo Rapid Line / JR Chuo-Sobu Line
exits.character: The way to the Junjo and Koshin-dori shopping streets. Shops selling fresh food and everyday goods line the way, and this is where daily life happens. There are plenty of bars too.

exits.name: South exit (南口)
exits.line: JR Chuo Rapid Line / JR Chuo-Sobu Line
exits.character: The Pal and Look shopping streets run south, and the vintage clothing shops are concentrated on this side. Many of the visitors are young, and at weekends the pavements stay busy from midday into the evening.

residents: Mostly students and people in their twenties and thirties living alone; the average age is low for a residential part of the 23 wards. Many run their own vintage shops or restaurants, and the shopkeepers still know one another. The share of families is low, so for anyone planning life around raising children, the late-night foot traffic and the number of places aimed at single people can feel like a poor fit.
housingStock: A high proportion of timber-built flats, and plenty of older, low-rent stock still on the market. Flats without a bath, or with the washing machine space outdoors, are still let here. Search for newer reinforced-concrete buildings and the choice narrows sharply, with rents no different from other Chuo Line stations. "Koenji is cheap" is a statement about old timber-built flats, and worth remembering as such.
hazards: On the national hazard map, for the flood scenario based on the largest rainfall the government models, the station itself falls outside the projected inundation area. Four of the nine points within 400 m of the station fall inside it, to a projected depth of 0.5 to 3 m. All of them lie on the southern side, where the ground falls towards the Kanda and Zenpukuji rivers. For the blocks of densely packed timber housing, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government publishes a fire-risk rating by neighbourhood in its regional hazard assessment, so look up the figure for the block you would live in. The projected depth differs block by block within the same station area, so check the ward hazard map for the specific address. Inland flooding from overwhelmed drains has no nationwide map; each ward publishes its own, and that is worth reading as well.
stationNote: The Chuo Rapid stops here on weekdays only and passes through at weekends and on holidays. On those days you are on the Sobu local line, which takes longer to reach Shinjuku. The north and south exits are reached after leaving the gates, and getting to the other side means the underpass or the level crossing.
nightWalk: The shopping streets are lit and busy until late, so walking home is not a worry. One street back, though, the timber-built residential blocks have narrow roads and few lamps. If you would rather not pass drinkers on the way home, choose a flat by whether the route takes you through the bar streets.
rentReason: Rent is low for somewhere eight minutes from Shinjuku. The reasons are the high share of older timber-built flats, the chronic morning crowding and delays on the Chuo Line, the spread of densely packed timber housing around the station, and the absence of any large shopping complex. Plenty of people choose the neighbourhood for its character, so compared on conditions alone it looks like a bargain.

rentRange.note: Within the same ten-minute walk, a timber-built flat with no bath and a newer reinforced-concrete flat differ by nearly double. Koenji's average looks low because there is so much of the former on the market; ask for ordinary fittings and the picture changes at once.

family: The share of households with children is not high, and both the shops and the housing lean towards people living alone. The ground is flat, on the terrace, so a pushchair is easy to manage, but there are few large parks near the station and Wadabori Park and the Zenpukuji riverside are some distance away. Check school catchment and nursery availability by address against Suginami City's own current information. Whether you read the late-night foot traffic as reassuring company or as noise that never lets up is what divides opinion here.
medical: Within walking distance of the station there are 25 clinics and 23 pharmacies, the most of any of the seventeen stations written up in this depth. Hojo Hospital is about 370 m away and Seizankai Kiyokawa Hospital about 550 m, so hospitals that admit inpatients are within walking distance too. For which clinics open at night and at weekends, ask the emergency advice line of the ward you live in.

alternatives.note: If you want quiet rather than bustle, choose Higashi-Nakano. Shinjuku is one stop away, but only local trains stop there. Rents are at a similar level.

If you want a train you can sit on in the morning, choose Sasazuka. Trains on the Keio New Line start there, and Shinjuku is five minutes away. The neighbourhood has nothing like Koenji's character, though.

outlook: No large redevelopment is on the horizon, and the make-up of the neighbourhood — vintage shops and restaurants at its centre — looks set to continue for the time being. On the other hand, disaster preparedness in densely packed timber housing is an acknowledged problem for the authorities, so over the long run rebuilding may reduce the stock of cheap timber-built flats.

residentComment: It is not a neighbourhood to recommend to everyone, but nowhere else in Tokyo packs this many vintage shops, live music venues and owner-run bars into one place, and anyone who wants that will struggle to find the same thing elsewhere. There are so many cheap places to eat that you can keep food costs down without cooking. The rent people call cheap, though, is a figure based on old timber-built flats; ask for ordinary fittings and it matches any other Chuo Line station. The morning crowding, and the Rapid passing through at weekends, are things you feel as an inconvenience most weeks once you live here. That this is a densely packed timber-housing area is worth facing squarely as the reason the rent is low.

neighbours.note: 828 m away in a straight line. It takes 3 minutes longer to reach Otemachi than Koenji.
1114 m away in a straight line. It reaches Otemachi in about the same time as Koenji. One-room rents run about ¥7,000 higher.

leads.terrain: The ground around the station is almost level, so you can choose where to live without thinking about slopes.
leads.groceries: There are 15 supermarkets within walking distance, and the nearest is 2 minutes on foot.
leads.hazards: Among the 23 wards' stations, comparatively few of the points around this one fall inside the projected inundation area for the largest rainfall the government models.
leads.stationNote: 2 lines serve the station. The choice of connections is about average for the 23 wards.
leads.rentRange: Set against how long the commute takes, rents here are among the lowest in the 23 wards.
leads.medical: The number of clinics and pharmacies within walking distance is among the highest in the 23 wards.
leads.exits: The north exit is the centre of everyday shopping, with fresh food and household goods; the second-hand clothes shops cluster on the south side.
